events.fact: The Articles of Confederation took effect when Maryland became the last state to ratify, binding the thirteen states into their first national union.
President Ulysses S. Grant signed the act establishing Yellowstone as the first national park, set aside as a public ground preserved from spoilation.

block: On March 1, 1781, the Articles of Confederation at last took force when Maryland became the thirteenth and final state to ratify, binding a quarrelsome people into their first governing union. On the same day in 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed the act setting aside Yellowstone as the first national park, a vast common trust kept from private spoilation for the generations to come. A Responsible citizen honors both labors, for the union that frames a nation and the land entrusted to it are alike held in stewardship before the God who gives every good thing to be guarded and not squandered.

events.fact: The delegates of Texas signed their Declaration of Independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos, founding a new republic.
The United States Congress passed the Act Prohibiting the Importation of Slaves, ending the legal importation of slaves effective January 1, 1808.

block: On March 2, 1836, the delegates of Texas signed their Declaration of Independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos, pledging their lives and sacred honor to a new and free republic on the open prairie. On the same day in 1807, the United States Congress passed the Act Prohibiting the Importation of Slaves, so that after two decades of constitutional delay the Republic finally obeyed the conscience that had long pricked it. Both days call an Obedient citizen to heed the higher law that binds the conscience, doing in his own hour the right his fathers could not yet accomplish.

events.fact: President John Tyler signed the act admitting Florida as the 27th state of the Union.
President Herbert Hoover signed the law making 'The Star-Spangled Banner' the national anthem of the United States.

block: On March 3, 1845, President John Tyler signed the act admitting Florida as the twenty-seventh state, drawing another commonwealth under the ordered government of the Union. On the same day in 1931, President Herbert Hoover signed the law that made 'The Star-Spangled Banner' the national anthem, fixing in law the song that had carried Americans through the rockets' red glare of war. An Obedient citizen takes his place in the ordered house of his country and lifts the common anthem, submitting his voice gladly to the lawful bonds that hold a free people together under God.

events.fact: The Boston Massacre occurred when British soldiers fired into a crowd, killing five colonists including Crispus Attucks.
George Westinghouse received the patent for his automatic railway air brake, a system that made rail travel vastly safer.

block: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a jeering Boston crowd and killed five colonists, a bloody hour that showed how quickly order collapses into death when restraint is cast off on both sides. On the same day in 1872, George Westinghouse received the patent for his automatic air brake, an invention that let a speeding train be halted at will and spared untold lives on the rails. An Obedient citizen learns from both that mastery lies in restraint, honoring the lawful order that holds violence in check and laboring, as Westinghouse did, to make the common path safe for his neighbor.

events.fact: Alexander Graham Bell was granted U.S. Patent 174,465 for the telephone.
The Battle of Pea Ridge opened in northwest Arkansas, where Union forces under General Samuel Curtis halted the Confederate advance and secured Missouri for the Union.

block: On March 7, 1876, the Patent Office granted Alexander Graham Bell patent number 174,465 for the telephone, the fruit of years of stubborn labor that would soon carry the human voice across a continent. On the same day in 1862, the Battle of Pea Ridge opened in the Arkansas hills, where General Samuel Curtis and his outnumbered men stood their ground through two days of fighting and broke the Confederate threat to Missouri. A Steadfast citizen presses on as Bell did at his workbench and as Curtis did on his line, refusing to yield until the work entrusted to him is finished.

events.fact: Alexander Graham Bell transmitted the first intelligible telephone speech, calling 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
The Salvation Army officially began its work in America when Commissioner George Scott Railton and seven women officers landed at New York and knelt to give thanks.

block: On March 10, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell spoke the first intelligible words ever carried by telephone, summoning his assistant with 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.' On the same day in 1880, Commissioner George Scott Railton and seven women officers of the Salvation Army stepped ashore at New York and knelt at once upon the dock to give God thanks before they began their mission to the poor. An Obedient citizen answers the call placed before him as Watson answered Bell's voice, and like those kneeling officers he begins every labor on his knees, ready to go where his Master sends him.

events.fact: The Continental Congress established the United States Army Corps of Engineers.
The Great Blizzard of 1888 struck the Northeast, burying the region in snow and claiming more than four hundred lives.

block: On March 11, 1779, the Continental Congress established the Army Corps of Engineers, the disciplined builders who would help fortify the young nation's defenses and later tame its rivers. On the same day in 1888, the Great Blizzard buried the Northeast under drifts that reached the rooftops and took more than four hundred lives, testing the endurance of every household from the Chesapeake to Maine. A Steadfast citizen learns from both that strength is forged in preparation and proven in the storm, building soundly in fair weather and holding fast when the snows come, trusting the God who is a refuge in the tempest.

events.fact: Juliette Gordon Low gathered the first troop of American Girl Scouts in Savannah, Georgia.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt delivered his first 'fireside chat' by radio, steadying a fearful nation during the banking crisis.

block: On March 12, 1912, Juliette Gordon Low gathered eighteen girls in Savannah to form the first American Girl Scout troop, founding a fellowship to train the young in service, skill, and duty. On the same day in 1933, in the depths of the Great Depression, President Franklin D. Roosevelt spoke his first fireside chat over the radio and quieted a panicked people with plain words about their banks. An Obedient citizen knows that small faithful duties and steady, honest counsel are how a people are led, and he gives himself to both, training the young and calming the fearful in the place God has set him.

events.fact: Eighteen-year-old Chester Greenwood of Maine received a patent for his improved earmuffs, an invention that long employed his hometown.
Benjamin Harrison, the twenty-third President of the United States, died at his home in Indianapolis at age sixty-seven.

block: On March 13, 1877, a Maine teenager named Chester Greenwood received a patent for the improved earmuff he had devised to keep his own ears warm, a humble invention that would keep his hometown employed for sixty years. On the same day in 1901, Benjamin Harrison, the twenty-third President and grandson of a president, died quietly at his home in Indianapolis, his term of service finished. An Obedient citizen honors the homely diligence of the young inventor and the faithful discharge of high office alike, knowing that God measures a man not by the size of his task but by his faithfulness in it.

events.fact: General George Washington delivered his Newburgh Address, quieting a threatened revolt among his officers and preserving civilian rule.
Maine was admitted to the Union as the twenty-third state.

block: On March 15, 1783, General George Washington walked unannounced into a meeting of his disgruntled officers at Newburgh and, fumbling for his spectacles, confessed he had grown gray and nearly blind in his country's service, and so shamed a brewing mutiny into submission to lawful authority. On the same day in 1820, Maine entered the Union as the twenty-third state, taking its ordered place among the commonwealths. An Obedient citizen reveres what Washington defended that day, the willing submission of sword to law, and like Maine he takes his appointed place within the lawful order God has appointed for a free people.

events.fact: British forces evacuated Boston after George Washington fortified Dorchester Heights, giving the Continental Army its first great victory.
Word of the victory prompted the Continental Congress to soon honor Washington with its first gold medal, 'Washington Before Boston.'

block: On March 17, 1776, eleven thousand British troops sailed out of Boston harbor after George Washington stole onto Dorchester Heights by night and crowned it with the cannon hauled from Ticonderoga, winning the Continental Army its first great victory without a battle. That same campaign moved the Continental Congress to strike its first gold medal in his honor, 'Washington Before Boston,' rewarding the patient obedience of a general who had besieged the city for eleven months. An Obedient citizen sees that the quiet, disciplined doing of one's duty, night after night upon the heights, is what God uses to deliver a people.

events.fact: Grover Cleveland, the only President to serve two non-consecutive terms, was born in Caldwell, New Jersey.
The British Parliament repealed the hated Stamp Act, yielding to the steadfast resistance of the American colonies.

block: On March 18, 1837, Grover Cleveland was born in Caldwell, New Jersey, the man who would become the only President to win the office twice in non-consecutive terms and who built his name on plain honesty and a willingness to stand alone with his vetoes. On the same day in 1766, the British Parliament repealed the despised Stamp Act, bowing to the firm and united resistance of colonists who would not be taxed without their consent. A Steadfast citizen takes heart from both, for Cleveland held his convictions against the crowd and the colonies held their ground against a king, and immovable conviction in a just cause is honored by God.

events.fact: President Woodrow Wilson signed the Standard Time Act, establishing the nation's time zones and daylight saving as a wartime measure.
The explorer Robert de La Salle was murdered by his own mutinous men near the Trinity River in present-day Texas.

block: On March 19, 1918, President Woodrow Wilson signed the Standard Time Act, ordering the whole nation onto common time zones so that a people at war might labor in step. On the same day in 1687, the great French explorer Robert de La Salle, who had claimed the Mississippi for empire, was shot dead by his own mutinous men on the banks of the Trinity River in what is now Texas. An Obedient citizen weighs the two ends, for one nation ordered itself willingly for the common good while one company cast off all authority and destroyed itself, and he chooses gladly the yoke of lawful order under God.

events.fact: Antislavery men met at Ripon, Wisconsin, in a gathering remembered as the founding of the Republican Party.
The USS Langley was commissioned as the United States Navy's first aircraft carrier.

block: On March 20, 1854, a band of citizens met in a little schoolhouse at Ripon, Wisconsin, and resolved to form a new party against the spread of slavery, a meeting long remembered as the birth of the Republican Party. On the same day in 1922, the Navy commissioned the USS Langley as America's first aircraft carrier, a daring experiment that launched the age of naval aviation. A Steadfast citizen honors both, for free men who plant a new institution upon conviction and sailors who pioneer an untried frontier both press forward in hope, building for a future they trust the providence of God to govern.

events.fact: The British Parliament passed the Stamp Act, the direct tax that first roused the American colonies to the cry of no taxation without representation.
A coordinated Powhatan attack on the Virginia settlements killed roughly a quarter of the Jamestown colony, which nevertheless endured.

block: On March 22, 1765, the British Parliament passed the Stamp Act, the first direct tax laid upon the colonies, which kindled the cry of no taxation without representation and steeled a people's resolve. On the same day in 1622, a sudden Powhatan assault swept the Virginia settlements and killed nearly a quarter of the Jamestown colonists, yet the battered colony held on and survived. An Enduring citizen takes both to heart, for a hard tax forged American resolve and a brutal morning could not extinguish a planted colony, and he learns to outlast every trial by the sustaining hand of God.

events.fact: Patrick Henry roused the Second Virginia Convention at St. John's Church in Richmond with the cry, 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'
Astronauts Gus Grissom and John Young flew Gemini 3, America's first two-man spaceflight and the first to maneuver a crewed craft in orbit.

block: On March 23, 1775, before the Second Virginia Convention gathered in St. John's Church in Richmond, Patrick Henry cast down his fears with the immortal cry, 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' and swung the colony toward armed defense. On the same day in 1965, Gus Grissom and John Young rode Gemini 3 into orbit on America's first two-man flight and steered their craft by hand among the stars, daring an untried frontier. A Steadfast citizen draws courage from the orator who staked his life on liberty and the astronauts who staked theirs on the unknown, resolving to hold his post whatever it costs, for the God who keeps him is faithful.

events.fact: Elvis Presley, at the height of his fame, was inducted into the United States Army and chose to serve as an ordinary soldier.
The tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Alaska's Prince William Sound, spilling some eleven million gallons of crude oil.

block: On March 24, 1958, Elvis Presley, the most famous young man in America, reported for induction into the United States Army and turned down a soft posting to serve as a plain soldier among his countrymen. On the same day in 1989, through a few minutes of negligence on watch, the tanker Exxon Valdez ran hard aground in Alaska's Prince William Sound and fouled hundreds of miles of coast with crude oil. An Obedient citizen sees in both that faithfulness in small duties is everything, for one man humbly took the common yoke while a single careless watch wrecked a wilderness, and he attends to the post God has given him.

events.fact: The colonists of the Ark and the Dove landed at St. Clement's Island, where Father Andrew White offered the first Catholic Mass in the English colonies and founded Maryland.
The Continental Congress resolved to strike its first gold medal, honoring George Washington for the liberation of Boston.

block: On March 25, 1634, the weary passengers of the Ark and the Dove came ashore at St. Clement's Island, where Father Andrew White raised a rough-hewn cross and offered the first Catholic Mass in the English colonies, planting Maryland as a refuge for conscience. On the same day in 1776, the Continental Congress resolved to strike its first gold medal in thanksgiving for Washington's deliverance of Boston. An Obedient citizen honors both acts of grateful obedience, the colonists who began their settlement at the altar and the Congress that paused to give honor where honor was due, ordering all his beginnings and victories alike under God.

events.fact: The Good Friday earthquake, magnitude 9.2 and the strongest ever recorded in North America, struck south-central Alaska and its coastal towns.
Juan Ponce de Leon sighted the coast of Florida near Easter and named the land 'La Pascua Florida,' the first European sighting of the future United States mainland.

block: On March 27, 1964, on Good Friday afternoon, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded on the continent, magnitude 9.2, shook south-central Alaska for nearly five minutes and loosed tsunamis upon its coastal towns. On the same day in 1513, near the feast of Easter, Juan Ponce de Leon first sighted the flowering coast of Florida and named it La Pascua Florida, the earliest European glimpse of the land that would become the United States. A Steadfast citizen marks how both fell within Holy Week, the ground convulsing on the day of the cross and a new shore revealed in the season of resurrection, and he stands unshaken upon the Rock that the trembling earth cannot move.

events.fact: A partial meltdown began at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, where operators labored for days to bring the reactor under control.
The frigate USS Essex under Captain David Porter fought two British warships at Valparaiso, Chile, surrendering only after a long and bloody resistance.

block: On March 28, 1979, a stuck valve and misread gauges brought a partial meltdown to the Three Mile Island reactor in Pennsylvania, and weary crews labored through anxious days and nights to master the wounded plant and spare the countryside. On the same day in 1814, the frigate USS Essex under Captain David Porter was cornered by two British men-of-war off Valparaiso and fought on against hopeless odds until, his decks running with blood, Porter at last struck his colors. A Steadfast citizen honors the engineers who would not abandon their posts and the sailors who would not yield until overpowered, learning to stand his ground in the long and costly hour, sustained by the God who never leaves his own.

events.fact: The last United States combat troops left South Vietnam as Hanoi released the remaining American prisoners of war.
John Tyler, the first Vice President to succeed to the presidency upon a President's death, was born in Charles City County, Virginia.

block: On March 29, 1973, the last American combat troops departed South Vietnam and the final prisoners of war came home, closing a long and bitter conflict borne by men who had endured much for their country. On the same day in 1790, John Tyler was born in Virginia, the man who upon the death of President Harrison would firmly establish that a Vice President fully becomes President, settling a grave constitutional question by standing on principle. A Steadfast citizen honors the soldiers who endured to the end of a hard war and the statesman who held a constitutional line under pressure, resolving to bear his own burdens faithfully to the last, as God gives strength.

events.fact: Secretary of State William Seward signed the treaty purchasing Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million, a bargain long mocked as 'Seward's Folly.'
Dr. Crawford Long of Jefferson, Georgia, performed the first surgery using ether anesthesia, painlessly removing a tumor from the neck of James Venable.

block: On March 30, 1867, in the small hours of the morning, Secretary of State William Seward signed the treaty buying Alaska from Russia for seven million dollars, a purchase derided as 'Seward's Folly' until time proved his foresight and steadfast vision. On the same day in 1842, a country doctor named Crawford Long in Jefferson, Georgia, gave ether to a patient and painlessly cut a tumor from his neck, the first surgery under anesthesia and a quiet mercy to all who would ever face the knife. A Steadfast citizen honors the statesman who held firm against ridicule and the physician who pressed on to ease his neighbor's suffering, persevering in good work though the world be slow to see its worth, for God rewards the faithful.
